buffer.title: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
buffer.text: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA Back to Articles An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 5 Vrunda Gadesha vrunda-gadesha Follow ibm-research Cyril Shaji cyrilshaji Follow ibm-research Jobit Treesa Varughese jotreesa1 Follow ibm-research Nivetha Suruliraj nivetha-suruliraj Follow ibm-research Anu Sugunan anu24-hugface Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Jaydeep Sen JaydeepSen Follow ibm-research Amith Singhee asinghee Follow ibm-research Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type. We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps . The use case: a Farm Assistant A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent: Listens and turns the speech into text. Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English. Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says. Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked. If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up. Where CUGA fits CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things: One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting. The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search() . Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's. The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it. audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server. The hard part is not the voice Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval : a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph. Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning. The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large ), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything. Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages. Making it sound right and keeping it safe A few small decisions mattered more than we expected: Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech. Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC , and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast. Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user. Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key. Try it You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer: CUGA Apps on Hugging Face → Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA , starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn. Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent. Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust. This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity. If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core . Learn more about CUGA New to CUGA? Here are some places to start: cuga.dev : the CUGA home page. CUGA on GitHub : the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue. CUGA documentation : setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration. CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub : the source for the apps in the Hugging Face Space. Spaces you can try in your browser: CUGA Agent : the general-purpose agent, running on a demo CRM scenario. CUGA Apps : launch working CUGA apps from one dashboard. CUGA Policy Playground : two live agents side by side, one with policies and one without. More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog: CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents : the introduction to CUGA and its configurable reasoning modes. Build real agentic apps using CUGA: two dozen working examples on a lightweight harness : the app gallery this voice agent belongs to. Same Model, Different Harness: CUGA, Hermes, and Deep Agents — When to Pick CUGA? : how much the harness matters when the model stays the same. buffer.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
buffer.text: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents Back to Articles Where scientists draw the line on AI agents Enterprise Article Published November 25, 2026 Upvote 5 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work. These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings. To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies. Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used. One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust : validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research. Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized. A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge. Helping researchers check the work For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually. But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs. Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis. But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way. Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows. These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks. These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like. Keep scientific judgment in the loop Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process? An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?” Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves. Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation. Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said. Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research. These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work. The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. buffer.title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
buffer.text: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems Back to Articles Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems Published November 26, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 16 +10 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Kashif Rasul kashif Follow Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models. That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50. Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents? In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from. First, we'll start off with some context on swarms. The rise of the swarms We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem. But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so. A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment , coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same. Did cooperation help, or did we just spend more? Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries. Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided. This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute? We understand that question through this simple expectation. Figure 1. Sketch of the expectation we want to test: compare communicating and independent agents at matched budgets. We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily. Multi-agent Systems and Reinforcement Learning Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms. A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture. This creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training. A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward. Agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are: A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog . A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL . Our first experiment: four agents ordering numbers We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows. Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is: #### [5, 5, 26, 78] The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list . One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates. This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful. The main communication tools are message(to, text) , read_messages() , and check_notifications() . A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone. We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy , with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments. Figure 2. The task and training loop. The private numbers illustrate a possible successful episode; this graphic is not a recorded conversation or a claim about the learned protocol at update 75. A team reward and eight attempts at each problem In this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens. For every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. week_log.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

Three datasets were open-sourced: Synthetic Charts V1, Synthetic Tables V1, and OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2.
The model supports multi-pass processing for high-density tables and charts.
Fine-tuning recipe provided for adapting the model to specific document types like dental forms.

facts: Hugging Face published a guide on building and training multi-agent systems.

Multi-agent systems face challenges like credit assignment and changing teammate policies.
Centralized training with decentralized execution is a common approach for multi-agent RL.

The study aims to determine if communication provides a performance boost over independent agents at matched budgets.
Initial experiments involve agents learning to share private integers to sort a list.

658331536.source: Artificial Analysis introduced AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 to evaluate frontier language models on controlling a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid robot. The benchmark includes ten household and industrial tasks across four skill groups: embodied reasoning, pick and place, assembly/tool use, and mobility. GPT-6.2 Astra leads the benchmark with a score of 71.0. Models are given five practice episodes in new scenes to write code and notes before being evaluated on ten additional unseen scenes. The simulation uses NVIDIA Isaac Sim and the Unitree G1 robot with 29 joints and three-fingered hands. Every model achieved a perfect score on the mobility task (warehouse navigation). Pick and place tasks were the weakest performance area for all models due to difficulties with the robot's three-fingered hands. GPT-6.2 Sol is the fastest model at 17.3 minutes per evaluation episode, while Claude Fable 5.2 is the most expensive at $9.01 per episode. Can language models drive a humanoid robot? Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 | Artificial Analysis Artificial Analysis K All articles November 25, 2026 Can language models drive a humanoid robot? Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 gives frontier language models control of a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid robot across ten household and industrial tasks. Today’s research preview of our simulation benchmark follows last month’s preview of AA-Robotics v0.1, our work with physical robot arms in our lab. In AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1, each model practices five episodes per task, keeps only the notes and code it wrote, and is then scored on ten new evaluation scenes with different rooms, lighting and task details. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 Frontier language models can now write and run code well enough to act in the physical world. AA-Robotics v0.1 was our first step, with models controlling a robot arm. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 evaluates frontier language models on their ability to control a simulated humanoid robot, which has to walk, look around, and use two dexterous hands at once. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 is our research preview of the simplest experiment we have designed to test this: language models in coding agent harnesses directly controlling a humanoid. Each model is given control of a simulated Unitree G1, with 29 joints, three-fingered hands and a head camera, and a simple objective for each task. It is the next step in our work measuring AI agents in simulated robotics, and we plan to expand from here. For each task, the model is first given five practice episodes back to back, each in a new scene, to learn the environment and take notes. Only the files it writes (memory, notes, code and skills) are kept. Using these, the model is then evaluated on ten new scenes, each with a different room, lighting, layout and task details, and each in a fresh run that starts from a copy of those files. We find that some skills are already mature, while others are missing from every model. Every model walked the robot to the goal without moving a package in every navigation episode, and most played the full melody on the toy piano in most episodes. But no model reliably loaded the dishwasher, with only five dishes ending in the rack in 90 episodes, and none finished with a single item of laundry in the washing machine. GPT-6.2 Astra leads AA-Robotics-Sim with 71.0, 13.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at 57.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol at 53.7. GPT-6.2 Astra succeeded in 61 of its 100 evaluation episodes, against 43 for Fable 5.2 and 41 for GPT-6.2 Sol, and was perfect on the toy piano, the abacus and the conveyor. A task's score is the mean of its 10 evaluation episodes, and the AA-Robotics-Sim score is the mean of the 10 task scores. Inference optimization on an RTX PRO 6000 achieved 190.6 tok/s using vLLM and DSpark. The model supports a 1M-token context window. Performance was improved by 40% compared to baseline configurations. The optimization process used a coding agent to run 46 benchmark experiments. Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000 Back to Articles Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000 Published November 25, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 1 Niels Rogge nielsr Follow Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here . One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs ( sm100 ), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ. We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint . Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs , and let it run experiments for an afternoon. Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb . The setup The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script ( bench.py ): Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning. Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs ( control → candidate → control ). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics. Log every run in PLAN.md , including regressions and dead ends. Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner. bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled. The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure: HF Jobs for compute. The rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver ( jobs/driver.py ) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls bench.py unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang ( lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini ) and vLLM nightly ( vllm/vllm-openai:nightly ) in parallel. CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap cpu-upgrade Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. What Parse 3.5 produces Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training : Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon Back to Articles Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon Team Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 14 +8 angt angt Follow ggml-org Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow ggml-org Abdennacer Badaoui badaoui Follow ggml-org The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware. Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance. Quick start You can choose Hardware , Model , and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201). In the Overview tab, compare quantizations for one hardware, model, and build. The two charts show PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens), both starting at context depth zero. In the Build history tab, track PP512 and TG128 across all recorded builds for the selected hardware, model, and quantization. In the Context scaling tab, see how token-generation throughput changes as the existing context grows, for the selected build, hardware, model, and quantization. What the numbers mean The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second: Test Workload What it helps you assess PP512 Process 512 input tokens How quickly the model processes a prompt TG128 Generate 128 tokens How quickly the model produces output Both tests start at context depth zero ( n_depth=0 ). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput ( avg_ts ). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows. How we run the benchmarks We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh , the build and installation project behind llama.app . The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration. The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M , Q8_0 , other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16 . Inspect and reuse the results The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model. Standard results use <build>/<hardware>/<model>/<quant>.jsonl . Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename. Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run. Identifying Molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Antigravity â Google DeepMind Skip to main content November 25, 2026 Science From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity Robert Brunck, Stefan Ganscha, Swaroop Guntupalli, Dariusz Lasecki, Gabriella Marfani, Jack Mason, Hussain Masoom, Rose Mirshafian, Eliseo Papa and Zoi Tsangalidou Explore Science on Google Antigravity Share Built in collaboration with analytical chemists and using community-developed tools, Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra, lay out chemical evidence, and match frontier-level retrieval accuracy even with a lightweight model. Every sample of blood, soil or plant tissue contains a vast array of small molecules, such as nutrients, hormones, drugs and their breakdown products, pollutants, or bioactive compounds with therapeutic potential. A modern mass spectrometer can detect tens of thousands of these molecular signals in a single drop of sample extract, measuring the masses of charged molecules and, in tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), the fragments they break into. These measurements, however, do not directly reveal the molecular structure. Researchers cannot immediately tell which compound produced a signal and relate it to its biological role or downstream use cases. To fully map the diversity of small molecules, which remains largely uncharted, researchers need ways to translate mass spectra to molecular structures at scale. The standard approach is to match each spectrum against reference spectra from previously measured molecules. Yet even after a decade of expanding reference libraries, spectral searches annotate on average only about 5% of measured spectra, and 10% for human samples; the rest has been called the "dark matter" of mass spectrometry. Many of the molecules producing these unannotated signals are already listed in public chemical databases, but their spectra have not been recorded, so there is no reference spectrum to compare against. Elucidating them instead requires inferring the structure directly from the observed fragment ions. Analytical chemists have a well-tested, step-by-step workflow for narrowing down candidate structures from tandem (MS/MS) spectra: check spectral reference libraries, find the molecular formula and retrieve candidate structures from chemical databases, and then test every candidate against observed fragment peaks. The tools for each step exist and are openly available, but running the full workflow would take a domain expert a significant amount of time for every single spectrum. Because a single study can produce thousands of spectra, manual analysis cannot keep up, leaving most of these signals unannotated. Today, we are sharing Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity , a suite of domain skills that pair Gemini's chemical reasoning with the ability to run established mass spectrometry tools and query public chemical databases on the user's behalf to fulfil their request. Antigravity runs these skills, combines their results, and reasons about the chemistry, laying out the evidence for a chemist to review. For molecules that are already catalogued in a database, identification is much faster. For undiscovered molecules, the agent still helps: it narrows down the formula and the parts of the structure supported by the fragments to guide full structure elucidation. A language model cannot do this on its own, since matching fragments to a structure takes precise mass calculations, searches across databases of millions of compounds, and simulations of how bonds break. Pairing Geminiâs reasoning with dedicated chemistry tools brings those steps into one workflow. Antigravity and the Mass Spec Skills have the potential to transform our natural product-based drug discovery workflows by substantially accelerating the identification of bioactive compounds from complex plant extracts. Their remarkable accuracy in predicting even highly complex molecular structures (>90% in most of our evaluations), coupled with detailed interpretation of MS/MS fragmentation patterns, could significantly reduce the time required for compound annotation and enable us to prioritise promising bioactive candidates more rapid

facts: NVIDIA released a Sim2Real workflow for Microduck obstacle avoidance using Isaac Lab and Newton.

The environment utilizes SimReady assets like cardboard boxes and office bins for obstacle course generation.
The MicroDuckToFCamera models a VL53L5CX sensor with an 8x8 grid at 15Hz.

month_log.title: From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity
facts: Google DeepMind introduced Mass Spec Skills for the Google Antigravity platform.
The tool uses Gemini's chemical reasoning to interpret tandem mass spectra.
It automates the workflow of identifying molecular structures from mass spectrometry data.
The system integrates with established tools like SIRIUS, MAGMa, MetFrag, and RDKit.

month_log.title: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
facts: IBM Research released an Indic Voice Agent built on the open-source CUGA agent harness.
The agent allows users to ask questions in regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu.
CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) handles agent wiring, tool management, and guardrails.
The system uses multilingual embedding models to enable cross-lingual retrieval between Indic languages and English documents.

month_log.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
facts: Inkling 2 Mini features ~26B total parameters with 3B active per token.
The model uses a looped Mixture-of-Experts architecture with 24 physical layers.
Inference optimization on an RTX PRO 6000 achieved 190.6 tok/s using vLLM and DSpark.
The model supports a 1M-token context window.

month_log.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
facts: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) interviewed 17 scientists on the responsible development of AI agents.
Five dimensions of scientific trust were identified: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency.
Researchers expressed concerns about AI agents overlooking conflicting evidence or making unsupported claims.
There is a need for clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted scientific work.

month_log.title: Can language models drive a humanoid robot? Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 November 25, 2026
facts: Artificial Analysis introduced AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 to evaluate frontier language models on controlling a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
The benchmark includes ten household and industrial tasks across four skill groups: embodied reasoning, pick and place, assembly/tool use, and mobility.
GPT-6.2 Astra leads the benchmark with a score of 71.0.
Models are given five practice episodes in new scenes to write code and notes before being evaluated on ten additional unseen scenes.

month_log.title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
facts: NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Parse for document-to-structured-data extraction.
The update includes synthetic training datasets, fine-tuning recipes, and DFlash2 speculator.
Training used supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
RLVR using GRPO reduced loop-flagged outputs by 77%.

month_log.title: Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon
facts: Hugging Face launched a benchmark dashboard for llama.cpp on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.
The dashboard tracks prompt processing (PP512) and text generation (TG128) performance.
Supported hardware includes Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).
Benchmarks are scheduled weekly using the llama-bench tool.

month_log.title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
facts: Hugging Face published a guide on building and training multi-agent systems.
The series focuses on training agents to communicate using small, affordable models.
Multi-agent systems face challenges like credit assignment and changing teammate policies.
Centralized training with decentralized execution is a common approach for multi-agent RL.
